source_reviews.independent_solution: As a proposed verification, measure the floating body's weight in air, tare a receiving vessel, set an overflow vessel to its settled overflow level, and let the body float freely without touching the vessel. Collect all liquid displaced and spilled by that flotation, then measure its net weight by subtracting the receiving vessel's tare. Static flotation gives F_A = G_body, and Archimedes gives F_A = G_displaced_liquid, so the two measured weights should agree within measurement uncertainty when air buoyancy is neglected. The body must actually float, all overflow must be collected off the weighing system, and no liquid should be lost by splashing or significant absorption. No measurement, uncertainty estimate or equality of experimental readings has actually been obtained.

source_reviews.independent_solution: For an initially stationary freely immersed object, F_A > G makes it start rising and F_A < G makes it start sinking. If F_A = G it may remain in equilibrium; for a fully immersed uniform solid in a homogeneous liquid this is rho_body = rho_liquid and permits equilibrium at any depth. A uniform solid with rho_body < rho_liquid rises while fully immersed, then its submerged volume decreases upon reaching the surface until F_A = G and it can float with part exposed. A uniform solid with rho_body > rho_liquid sinks. Thus final surface flotation is an equality of forces with partial immersion, not the continued inequality F_A > G.

source_reviews.independent_solution: The unconditional result is V_submerged / V_total = rho_body / rho_liquid: in one liquid, greater body density requires a larger submerged fraction. source_reviews.independent_solution: A heavy ship can have a large hollow, air-containing hull and displace a correspondingly large mass of water. It floats when it can displace M_ship/rho_water of water before flooding, so F_A reaches its weight. Neither total mass alone nor the density of the hull metal decides flotation; the whole object's effective mass relative to its usable displaced volume matters. A small solid nail has little displaced volume and, for a metal denser than water such as the iron of selected block 12, G_nail > rho_water * g * V_nail even when wholly submerged, so it sinks. This is not a claim that every heavy vessel floats regardless of its load, hull integrity or available freeboard.

source_reviews.independent_solution: The general single-liquid solution is exhaustive: for each of the three solid spheres, compare its material density with the liquid; less means surface flotation, greater means sinking until contact, equal means neutral interior equilibrium. Under the additionally supplied hierarchy rho_cork < rho_kerosene < rho_paraffin < rho_water < rho_steel < rho_mercury, three separate single-liquid vessels would give nine outcomes: cork floats in water, kerosene and mercury; paraffin floats in water and mercury but sinks in kerosene; steel sinks in water and kerosene but floats in mercury. Under that same hierarchy, a sufficiently deep single three-layer vessel would instead put cork at the upper kerosene/air surface, paraffin across the kerosene/water interface, and steel across the water/mercury interface. For a sphere crossing only adjacent layers, rho_body*V_total = rho_upper*V_upper + rho_lower*V_lower; hence paraffin's fraction in water is (rho_paraffin-800)/(1000-800), and steel's fraction in mercury is (rho_steel-1000)/(rho_mercury-1000). This assumes adequate layer thickness and no wall or bottom support; large spheres can span more layers, requiring the corresponding sum over all submerged portions. The seed does not explicitly choose the separate-vessel or layered-vessel reading, does not supply cork/paraffin/steel density data, and does not give sphere sizes or layer depths. source_reviews.independent_solution: The actual figures show an inverted, open-bottom diver containing trapped air and some water, with a weight, inside surrounding water. In fig-170 a pressed membrane raises container pressure; in fig-171 the tube opens into the bottle's headspace above the water. A pressure increment is transmitted through the liquid, illustrating Pascal's law, and compresses the diver's trapped gas so water enters through the bottom opening. One consistent force accounting treats the rigid outer envelope plus its contained water as the body: when it is wholly immersed, exterior displaced volume and F_A are approximately fixed but admitted water increases body mass and G, eventually giving G > F_A and sinking. Reducing pressure expands the gas, expels water and lowers that body's G; if F_A > G it rises, and at the surface reduced immersion yields F_A = G. Alternatively, for fixed dry glass/ballast plus trapped gas, exclude the interior water from the body: the effective displaced volume is glass plus gas, so gas compression lowers buoyancy at approximately fixed dry weight. These are alternative consistent system boundaries, not simultaneous claims that both independent changes apply to the same body definition. Adjusted equal forces can give neutral equilibrium at a selected submerged depth in the ideal model; this is not proof of automatic stable equilibrium at every depth, because gas compression depends on pressure and depth. This explains Pascal transmission, Archimedean force and float/sink relations. Construction, pressure adjustments, demonstrations and historical mouth-blowing experiments have not been carried out or safety-approved.
